Question: Consider a sequence \(x_1,\) \(x_2,\) \(x_3,\) \(\ldots,\) defined by \[ \begin{aligned} x_1&=\sqrt[3]{3},\\ x_2&=(\sqrt[3]{3})^{\sqrt[3]{3}}. \end{aligned} \] and in general \[ x_n=(x_{n-1})^{\sqrt[3]{3}} \] for \(n\gt1.\) What is the smallest value of \(n\) for which \(x_n\) is an integer?
Solution:
Write \(c=\sqrt[3]{3}>1\). All terms are positive, so successive powers can be combined by multiplying their exponents. The first four terms are
\[
x_1=c,\qquad x_2=c^c,\qquad
x_3=c^{c^2},\qquad x_4=c^{c^3}=c^3=3.
\]
Thus \(n=4\) works. To prove it is the first such index, we must exclude the preceding three terms.

Since \(3<(3/2)^3\), we have \(1<c<3/2\), so \(1<x_1<2\). Because the base \(c\) is greater than \(1\), increasing an exponent increases the power. Hence
\[
1<x_2=c^c<c^{3/2}=\sqrt{c^3}=\sqrt3<2.
\]
Also, \((c^2)^3=9\), and \(8<9<27\), so \(2<c^2<3\). Comparing exponents with base \(c\) now gives
\[
2<c^2<c^{c^2}=x_3<c^3=3.
\]
Each earlier term lies strictly between consecutive integers. Therefore the smallest index is \(\boxed{4}\), choice C.
